backlog.title: What Can Go Wrong In 800VDC AI Data Centers
backlog.summary:
Sparks and fires caused by higher electrical currents can cause costly outages and put people in danger. Hot chips also cause problems. 
The post What Can Go Wrong In 800VDC AI Data Centers appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Data centers are transitioning to 800V DC power distribution to support high-density AI racks, which can reach 1 megawatt per rack.
Higher voltages improve efficiency and thermal performance through wide bandgap semiconductors like GaN, but they significantly increase the risk of dangerous power arcs during hot-swapping.
Reliability in 800V environments requires advanced isolation and protective hot-swap circuitry to prevent catastrophic equipment failure and ensure worker safety.

backlog.title: Humanoid Compute, Security More Complex Than AVs
backlog.summary:
Robots and autonomous vehicles are both edge devices, but a humanoid has wheels as well as fingers. Close interaction with humans raises the stakes. 
The post Humanoid Compute, Security More Complex Than AVs appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: The U.S. robotics market reached $11.4 billion in 2026, with humanoid development increasingly relying on AI-native architectures rather than retrofitted hardware.
Humanoid compute architectures are evolving into hybrid models, featuring a central AI unit for high-level planning and zonal microcontrollers for real-time, safety-critical actuation.
Safety in humanoid robotics requires a certified hardware-based 'safety companion' that operates independently of the AI model to ensure fault tolerance.

backlog.title: Building Trust Into Physical AI Systems
backlog.summary:
Security and safety are inseparable in the physical world.
The post Building Trust Into Physical AI Systems appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Physical AI systems, such as autonomous vehicles and industrial robots, require higher reliability standards because errors can lead to direct physical harm.
Security vulnerabilities in physical AI extend beyond software to include training data bias and sensor spoofing, which can degrade perception and decision-making.
Trust in physical AI must be built across the entire chain, from initial data ingestion and sensor input to the final physical actuation.

backlog.title: Protecting Mission-Critical Data Beyond The SoC: Why Inline Memory Encryption Needs Integrity
backlog.summary:
Aerospace and government systems need confidentiality, authentication, and implementation resilience for off-chip memory.
The post Protecting Mission-Critical Data Beyond The SoC: Why Inline Memory Encryption Needs Integrity appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Inline Memory Encryption (IME) is essential for protecting sensitive data as it moves between the SoC and off-chip memory, a critical attack surface.
Encryption alone is insufficient for mission-critical systems because it does not prevent attackers from altering data, which can lead to system-level manipulation.
Security architects must implement authentication alongside encryption to ensure data integrity, particularly for AI models where poisoned inputs can compromise inference results.

backlog.title: Agriculture relies on fossil fuels. It’s costing us.

But farmers buying fertilizer for their crops are especially aware of just how far the ripple effects of the conflict in Iran have spread. Fertilizer prices have been on a…
bullets: Fertilizer production is deeply tied to fossil fuel markets, as natural gas serves as both an energy source and a primary chemical feedstock for ammonia.
The conflict in Iran has disrupted the Strait of Hormuz, a critical transit route for one-third of global seaborne fertilizer trade, exacerbating price volatility.
Urea prices reached $850 per metric ton in April, an 80% increase compared to pre-conflict levels, highlighting the vulnerability of agricultural inputs to geopolitical instability.
Fertilizer manufacturing accounts for approximately 2% of global greenhouse gas emissions, prompting increased interest in climate-friendly alternatives like genetically edited microbes.

backlog.title: Architecting memory and storage in the AI era
backlog.summary: The era of AI inference has arrived. Imagine a healthcare system analyzing millions of data points in real time to accelerate life-saving medical research, or an intelligent assistant instantly resolving thousands of complex customer needs at once. These real-world breakthroughs rely on advanced infrastructure acting as the engine of continuous intelligence, powering real-time services while…
bullets: The shift toward AI inference workloads necessitates a fundamental redesign of enterprise infrastructure, moving away from legacy systems to prioritize memory bandwidth, storage throughput, and networking.

Industry experts emphasize that AI is not a monolithic workload but a diverse set of billions of processes, requiring infrastructure that balances performance per watt with scalability and real-time responsiveness.
Organizations must move beyond siloed optimization to create coordinated, purpose-built architectures that can handle the geographically distributed and latency-sensitive nature of modern agentic AI.
For business leaders, the primary strategic challenge is balancing infrastructure costs and environmental footprint while removing memory and storage bottlenecks that currently limit AI growth.

backlog.title: Why Biotech Companies Go to Australia to Test New Drugs
backlog.summary: How America can get promising drugs into human trials faster, at lower cost, and without sacrificing safety
bullets: Biotech firms are increasingly shifting Phase I clinical trials to Australia to bypass U.S. regulatory hurdles that can delay trial initiation by 18 to 24 months.
While the FDA's 30-day IND review period is not the primary bottleneck, ambiguous and non-risk-proportionate manufacturing requirements in the U.S. create significant administrative friction.
Australia's clinical trial environment offers a faster, more cost-effective pathway for early-stage human testing while maintaining equivalent safety standards.

The U.S. government is exploring reforms through 'Operation TrialBlazer' and the FDA's Expedited IND pilot, which aim to emulate the Australian model to improve domestic clinical trial competitiveness.

backlog.title: How Many Design Experiments Does A Machine Learning Predictor Actually Need?
backlog.summary:
Required dataset size and achievable accuracy track how smooth the response is, not model size or number of design variables. 
The post How Many Design Experiments Does A Machine Learning Predictor Actually Need? appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: The number of experiments required to train an ML predictor in CAE is determined by the smoothness of the response function rather than the number of design variables.
Discontinuous responses, such as integer counts of damaged battery cells, require significantly larger datasets to achieve predictive accuracy compared to smooth functions like mass.
Engineers should prioritize the nature of the physical response when planning simulation budgets, as model size does not correlate with the training data requirements.

backlog.title: This founder is making cheaper, cleaner steel
backlog.summary: The steel industry isn’t exactly known for innovation. Very little has changed about purifying iron ore since the process was invented and commercialized in the 1850s. The majority of steelmakers melt solid iron ore at dizzyingly high temperatures inside blast furnaces, where the material reacts with gases to trigger chemical reactions that remove oxygen. It…
bullets: Hertha Metals has developed a single-step furnace process that replaces coal with natural gas to refine iron ore into liquid steel.
The technology claims to reduce carbon emissions by at least 50% while simultaneously cutting production costs by 25% compared to traditional blast furnace methods.
Given that steel production accounts for roughly 7% of global carbon emissions, this innovation offers a scalable path to decarbonization that aligns with the industry's tight profit margins.

backlog.title: Research Bits: Sept. 8
backlog.summary:

bullets: Researchers at the National University of Singapore developed an amorphous carbon film that acts as both a low-k insulator (k=1.35) and a copper barrier at thicknesses as low as 0.8nm.

backlog.title: Write Things Down
backlog.summary: Writing things down is powerful, for humans and for AI; what comes first, however, is what to write, why to do it, and actually getting things done.
bullets: The author draws a parallel between human short-term memory and computer RAM, arguing that unorganized tasks create mental overload that hinders cognitive performance.
David Allen’s 'Getting Things Done' methodology emphasizes offloading incomplete tasks into a trusted external system to free up mental bandwidth for focus.
The post highlights the historical intersection of productivity software and hardware, noting how tools like OmniFocus attempted to digitize these organizational workflows.
The author reflects on the evolution of his own workflow since launching Stratechery in 2013, transitioning from complex systems to a focus on core content creation and operational management.
